findings.body: Interpolating user_name into a shell command changes literal argument handling into shell parsing. Names containing spaces are split into multiple arguments, and shell metacharacters can execute additional commands. Restore the argument-list invocation to preserve behavior and avoid command injection.
findings.failure_scenario: A user_name such as 'alice; touch /tmp/report-injected' executes an additional command under the application's privileges instead of being passed literally to report.
findings.title: Pass the user name as an argument without invoking a shell

findings.body: The new slice silently removes the first row from every nonempty result, contradicting the stated goal of preserving report behavior. The original function returned the supplied rows unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: When rows contains a single report entry and the subprocess succeeds, render_report now returns an empty list, losing that entry from the result.
findings.title: Return all rows rather than dropping the first

findings.body: The replacement assertion accepts any non-None result, including an empty list or rows that are dropped, reordered, or corrupted. This removes the existing row-preservation regression check. Retain a content assertion; if the report's intended return format has changed, assert the corresponding expected output instead.
findings.title: Assert the report's expected contents, not just its presence

findings.body: The switch from an argument list to a shell command has no accompanying test of subprocess invocation. Add a test with spaces and shell metacharacters that verifies the user name remains a single literal argument and shell interpretation is disabled. Recording the subprocess call avoids executing the supplied command while testing the invocation constructed by render_report.
findings.suggestion:
def test_render_report_passes_user_name_literally(monkeypatch) -> None:
    import subprocess

    calls = []

    def record_run(command, **kwargs):
        calls.append((command, kwargs))

    monkeypatch.setattr(subprocess, "run", record_run)
    user_name = "Alice Smith; echo unexpected"
    render_report(user_name, ["first", "second"])

    assert len(calls) == 1
    command, kwargs = calls[0]
    assert command == ["report", "--user", user_name]
    assert kwargs.get("shell", False) is False
    assert kwargs.get("check") is True

findings.anchor: export function fetchUser(id: string, timeoutMs: number): [Record<string, unknown>, number] {
findings.body: Making timeoutMs required contradicts the stated compatibility goal. Existing TypeScript calls with only an id no longer compile, and JavaScript calls that omit the argument receive undefined instead of the previous 30000 value. Retain the default parameter.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing fetchUser("123") call fails TypeScript argument checking; in JavaScript, the omitted timeout is no longer defaulted to 30000.
findings.title: Preserve the optional timeout and its default

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: Returning a tuple instead of the original record breaks the promised compatibility: id, timeoutMs, and fetchedAt are no longer properties of the returned value. Restore the record return value and its return annotation rather than requiring callers to destructure a new API.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller reading fetchUser("123", 1000).id gets undefined at runtime instead of "123"; typed property access also fails compilation.
findings.title: Retain the object return shape

findings.body: execSync interprets the interpolated userName as shell syntax rather than a single argument. Names containing spaces are split, and shell metacharacters can execute arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. Restore the spawnSync import and argument-array invocation instead of constructing a shell command.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller supplies a userName such as "alice; touch /tmp/report-injected", causing an additional command to execute rather than treating the entire value as the user name.
findings.title: Pass the user name as an argument without invoking a shell

findings.body: Interpolating userName into a command executed by execSync makes shell syntax in the name executable, whereas the previous spawnSync call passed it as a literal argument. If a caller supplies an attacker-controlled name, this permits arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. Restore the spawnSync import and argument-array invocation, or use execFileSync with separate arguments.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies userName as `alice; touch /tmp/report-injected`; execSync runs both the report command and the injected command under the application's account.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by passing arguments without a shell

findings.body: slice(1) unconditionally removes the first row, whereas the previous implementation returned every row. No header distinction is made, so this changes the report contents rather than keeping them stable.
findings.failure_scenario: A report containing one data row now returns an empty array, and every nonempty report loses its first row.
findings.title: Return all rows rather than dropping the first

findings.body: The truthiness assertion accepts any array, including an empty array, so it no longer checks the row-preservation contract covered by the original test. In particular, it cannot detect the newly introduced removal of the first row. Retain the exact contents assertion rather than weakening coverage alongside the behavior change.
findings.title: Restore an exact assertion on the returned rows

findings.body: Canonicalization and the prefix check validate a pathname, not the file subsequently opened. If an attacker can modify entries beneath the report root, they can replace the checked file or an ancestor directory with a symlink before File::open resolves it again, bypassing the containment check. Open relative to a trusted directory handle using enforced beneath-root resolution (such as Linux openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH), or an equivalent race-resistant approach.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with write access beneath the report root swaps a checked entry for a symlink to an outside file between canonicalize and File::open, causing open_report to return an out-of-root file readable by the process.
findings.title: Prevent TOCTOU path traversal with a directory-relative open

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: Concatenating `user` into a `/bin/sh -c` command makes shell metacharacters executable rather than treating the value as a single argument. If a caller controls this value, they can execute arbitrary commands with the service's privileges. Restore the argument-separated ProcessBuilder invocation without a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller supplies `alice; touch /tmp/report-injected` as `user`, causing the shell to execute both the report command and the injected command under the service account.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by passing user as a separate argument

findings.body: Starting the sublist at index 1 discards the first row on every nonempty result, contradicting the stated goal of preserving rows. For an empty list, the range is inverted and throws IllegalArgumentException. Returning rows preserves both the contents and the previously supported empty-list behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A one-row report becomes empty, larger reports lose their first row, and an empty report throws instead of returning an empty list.
findings.title: Return all report rows without slicing

findings.body: The replacement assertion checks only that a list exists, so it no longer verifies row contents or ordering. This removes the regression coverage precisely where render now slices the supplied rows. Retain the original preservation assertion rather than allowing a non-null but truncated result to satisfy the test.
findings.title: Restore the assertion on returned row contents

findings.body: The pull_request_target event runs in the base repository's security context, but this checkout selects contributor-controlled code. The subsequent npm test executes scripts from that code with RELEASE_TOKEN in its environment. A fork PR can modify package.json to steal the token; contents: read does not restrict this separately supplied secret. Run PR tests under pull_request without repository secrets, and keep any privileged release operations in a separate trusted workflow that does not execute PR code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a fork PR with a malicious npm test script; the target workflow checks out that commit and executes the script with RELEASE_TOKEN, allowing the attacker to exfiltrate the credential.

findings.body: Rejecting only the literal `0.0.0.0/0` does not enforce the stated prohibition on public admin access. For example, `128.0.0.0/1` passes this validation and configures SSH ingress from half the IPv4 address space, replacing the previous fixed private range. Validate membership in approved administrative networks (or use an explicit allowlist) rather than excluding one string.

findings.body: Interpolating user_name into a shell command changes literal argument handling into shell parsing. Names containing spaces are split into multiple arguments, and shell metacharacters can execute arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. Restore the argument-list invocation to preserve behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name such as 'alice; touch /tmp/report-injected' causes the shell to execute an additional command instead of treating the entire value as the user name.
findings.title: Pass the user name as an argument without invoking a shell

findings.body: The new slice unconditionally discards the first row, although the previous implementation returned the complete list and the stated intent promises to preserve behavior. A single-row report now returns no rows.
findings.failure_scenario: When rows contains ['first', 'second'], the function returns only ['second'], silently omitting report data.
findings.title: Return all report rows

findings.body: Replacing exact equality with a non-None check weakens the existing behavioral contract despite the stated goal of preserving report behavior. This test now accepts empty, reordered, or otherwise incorrect output. Keep the exact expected rows assertion while exercising the user-name argument.
findings.title: Retain the row-preservation assertion

findings.body: The change from argument-list execution to shell execution has no corresponding test of command construction. Add a test with spaces and shell metacharacters that checks the name is passed as a single literal argument without enabling a shell. Mock only the subprocess boundary so the test exercises render_report without executing an external command.

    with patch("report.subprocess.run") as run:
        render_report(user_name, ["first", "second"])
    run.assert_called_once_with(["report", "--user", user_name], check=True)

findings.body: execSync interprets the interpolated userName as shell syntax, whereas the previous spawnSync call passed it as a literal argument. If a caller supplies an attacker-controlled name, shell metacharacters can execute arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. Restore spawnSync with an argument array, or import execFileSync and pass the executable and arguments separately.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies userName as "alice; touch /tmp/injected", causing the shell to run both report and the injected command under the application's account.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by passing arguments without a shell

findings.body: Interpolating userName into a command executed by execSync gives shell syntax special meaning. Names containing spaces no longer arrive as a single argument, and shell metacharacters can execute additional commands. Restore an argument-array invocation with spawnSync (including its import) rather than building a shell command.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling renderReport with a name such as "alice; touch /tmp/report-injected" executes an additional command instead of passing the complete name to report.
findings.title: Pass the user name as an argument without invoking a shell

findings.body: slice(1) removes the first row from every nonempty result, contradicting the existing preservation behavior and the stated intent to keep report output stable. A single-row report now returns an empty array. The weakened truthiness assertion also allows this regression to pass; retain the exact array comparison.
findings.failure_scenario: When renderReport receives ["first", "second"] and the command succeeds, it returns only ["second"], omitting report data.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first

findings.body: The truthiness assertion accepts any array, including an empty one, so it no longer checks the row-preservation contract exercised by the original test. In particular, it cannot detect the newly introduced removal of the first row via `rows.slice(1)`. Restore the exact-content assertion rather than weakening coverage alongside the behavior change.
findings.title: Restore an assertion on the returned rows

findings.body: Canonicalization and the prefix check validate a pathname, not the file subsequently opened. If another process can modify entries beneath root, it can replace the validated file or an ancestor directory with a symlink before File::open resolves the path again, bypassing the containment check. Use a directory-handle-relative open with containment enforced during resolution (for example, Linux openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH), or an equivalent platform-specific safe traversal.
findings.failure_scenario: An actor with write access beneath root swaps a checked path component for a symlink between canonicalize and File::open, causing open_report to return a file outside root despite the successful prefix check.
findings.title: Enforce containment during the file open, not before it

findings.body: Concatenating `user` into a command interpreted by `/bin/sh -c` allows shell metacharacters and command substitutions to execute rather than remain argument data. If an attacker can influence `user`, this permits arbitrary commands with the service's privileges. Restore the argument-based ProcessBuilder invocation so the value is not parsed by a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies `user` as `alice; touch /tmp/report-injected`; the shell runs both the report command and the attacker-specified command under the service account.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by passing user as a separate argument

findings.body: Starting the sublist at index 1 discards the first row, contradicting the stated goal of preserving rows. It also creates an invalid range for an empty list, turning a previously valid result into an exception.
findings.failure_scenario: Two input rows return only the second row, a singleton returns no rows, and an empty list throws IllegalArgumentException because the start index exceeds the end index.
findings.title: Return all report rows without slicing

findings.body: Replacing the equality assertion with assertNotNull removes coverage of row contents and ordering precisely when render changes which rows it returns. The assertion accepts an empty or truncated list, so it cannot detect unintended row loss. Retain an explicit expected-list assertion; if dropping the first row is intentional, specify that contract explicitly rather than checking only non-nullness.
findings.title: Restore the assertion on returned row contents

findings.body: Concatenating user into a command interpreted by sh allows shell metacharacters and command substitutions to execute arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. Restore direct execution with a separate argument so user is treated as data rather than shell syntax.
findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker supplies user as "alice; touch /tmp/report-injected", Render executes the injected touch command in addition to report.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by passing user as an argument

findings.body: `rows[1:]` discards the first report row, contradicting the stated intent to preserve rows. It also panics for a nil slice or an empty slice with zero capacity, whereas the previous return handled both safely. Return the original slice.
findings.failure_scenario: A report with one row returns no rows, and a nil rows input causes a slice-bounds panic instead of returning normally.
findings.title: Return all rows rather than slicing off the first

findings.body: The non-None assertion accepts any list, including an empty or truncated one, so it no longer checks the row-preservation contract covered by the original test. findings.body: The subprocess invocation changes from an argument list to shell interpretation, but the accompanying test only supplies a simple name and does not inspect the invocation. Add a regression test with shell metacharacters that verifies the user name is passed as a single literal argument without enabling a shell. Mocking the subprocess boundary avoids executing an external command while still exercising render_report's command construction.

    with patch("report.subprocess.run") as run:

findings.body: The command interpolates userName directly into a string executed by execSync through a shell. Unlike the previous spawnSync argument array, this interprets shell metacharacters and command substitutions as executable syntax. If a caller supplies an attacker-controlled user name, it can execute arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. Restore spawnSync with separate arguments, or import execFileSync and pass the executable and arguments separately.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a userName such as `alice; touch /tmp/report-injected`; execSync executes the injected command as well as report.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by passing arguments without a shell

findings.body: Interpolating userName into an execSync command changes it from a literal argument into shell syntax. Names containing spaces are split into multiple arguments, and shell metacharacters can execute additional commands. Restore the spawnSync import and argument-array invocation to preserve named-user behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A userName such as "alice; touch /tmp/report-injected" causes the shell to execute an additional command rather than treating the entire name as the --user value.
findings.title: Pass the user name as an argument without invoking a shell

findings.body: slice(1) discards the first row on every successful invocation. This contradicts preserving report behavior and turns a single-row report into an empty report.
findings.failure_scenario: When the command succeeds and rows is ["first", "second"], the function returns only ["second"], silently omitting the first report entry.
findings.title: Return all supplied report rows

findings.body: `toBeDefined()` accepts any defined result, including an empty array, so it no longer tests the returned rows. In particular, it cannot detect the accompanying change from `rows` to `rows.slice(1)`, which removes the first row. Keep the exact-content assertion to cover the row-preservation contract rather than merely checking that a value exists.
findings.title: Restore the assertion on the returned report rows

findings.body: execSync interprets the interpolated userName through a shell, whereas the previous spawnSync call passed it as a single argument. Shell metacharacters in a caller-controlled name can now execute arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. Restore spawnSync with an argument array and its import, or use execFileSync with separate arguments.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies userName as "alice; touch /tmp/report-injected", causing the shell to execute both report and the attacker-specified command.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by avoiding shell execution

findings.body: Interpolating userName into a command executed by execSync changes it from a literal argument to shell syntax. Names containing spaces are split into multiple arguments, and shell metacharacters can execute additional commands. Restore the spawnSync import and argument-array invocation to preserve named-user behavior without shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: A userName such as "alice; touch /tmp/report-injected" executes an additional command, while "Alice Smith" no longer reaches report as one user argument.
findings.title: Pass the user name as an argument without a shell

findings.body: slice(1) unconditionally removes the first row, contradicting the existing preservation behavior and the stated goal of keeping report output stable. A single-row report now returns an empty array.
findings.failure_scenario: When rows is ["first", "second"], renderReport returns only ["second"], omitting a report row.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first

findings.body: Replacing equality with truthiness weakens the existing check precisely where the stated intent promises stable output for named users. An empty array, reordered rows, or an unrelated truthy value now passes this test. Retain the exact expected-output assertion so this test continues to verify stability rather than merely a truthy return value.
findings.title: Retain the exact row assertion for output stability

findings.body: The previous implementation returned the repository's batch result without filtering. The new conditions silently discard inactive records, records without an owner, and records with a disabled owner. This changes which requested records callers receive, rather than merely changing how they are loaded. Preserve the existing result semantics unless this filtering is an explicit API requirement.
findings.failure_scenario: When a requested record previously returned by loadMany is inactive or lacks an enabled owner, enrich now omits it, leaving callers with an incomplete result.
findings.title: Preserve the previously returned records

findings.body: Replacing loadMany(ids) with an awaited load(id) inside the loop introduces one serial repository call per ID. For an I/O-backed repository, latency accumulates across all lookups instead of using the existing batch interface. Load the items with loadMany once, then apply the filtering to those results.
findings.failure_scenario: With many IDs and an I/O-backed repository, each lookup waits for the previous one to finish, causing total enrichment latency to grow with the sum of individual lookup latencies.
findings.title: Retain the batch load before filtering

findings.body: ResultArrayFactory only wraps an empty array literal and has a single caller. It adds an unnecessary abstraction to a built-in operation. Replace this call with an array literal and remove the factory class.
findings.title: Create the result array directly

findings.body: The interpolated user value is now parsed by `sh -c`, so shell metacharacters and command substitutions execute rather than remaining literal argument data. Restore direct invocation of `report` with separate arguments and remove the unused command string.
findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker supplies `alice; touch /tmp/report-injected` as user, the shell executes the additional command with the application's privileges.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by passing user as a direct argument

findings.body: The added skip discards the first row of every nonempty report, contradicting the stated goal of preserving rows. The weakened test now accepts this incorrect result; restore its exact row equality assertion as well.
findings.failure_scenario: Passing two rows returns only the second, and passing a single row returns an empty report.
findings.title: Return all report rows without skipping the first

findings.body: The nonempty assertion accepts a result containing only one of the two input rows, so it no longer checks preservation, ordering, or exact contents alongside the changed row-processing code. Restore exact equality and cover a single-row input as well.
findings.suggestion:
assert_eq!(render_report("alice", vec!["first".into(), "second".into()]), vec!["first", "second"]);
    assert_eq!(render_report("alice", vec!["only".into()]), vec!["only"]);
findings.title: Restore assertions for the complete returned rows

findings.body: The command invocation now passes the interpolated user through `sh -c`, but the accompanying test exercises only `alice`. Add a regression test checking that shell syntax supplied as user data cannot create an unrelated file.
findings.title: Add coverage for shell metacharacters in the user argument

findings.body: Canonicalization and the prefix check validate a pathname, not the object subsequently opened. If another process can modify entries under the root, it can replace the validated file or an ancestor directory with a symlink before File::open resolves that pathname, bypassing the new containment check. Use a directory-handle-relative open with enforced beneath-root resolution (such as openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH on Linux), or an equivalent secure component walk.
findings.failure_scenario: An actor with write access under root replaces a validated entry with a symlink to an outside file between canonicalize and File::open, causing open_report to return a file outside root despite the prefix check.
findings.title: Enforce containment during the file open

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: Replacing the argument-vector invocation with `/bin/sh -c` makes the user value shell source rather than a single argument. Spaces alter argument boundaries and shell metacharacters can execute additional commands. This security-relevant change is unrelated to the stated goal of preserving report rows; retain the original ProcessBuilder invocation.
findings.failure_scenario: If user is `alice; touch /tmp/report-injected`, the shell runs both report and touch instead of passing the entire value as the report user.
findings.title: Keep the user argument out of shell interpretation

findings.body: Starting the sublist at index 1 discards the first row on every nonempty input, contradicting the stated goal of preserving rows. For an empty list, the start index exceeds the end index and the method throws IllegalArgumentException rather than returning an empty result. Return rows unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: A one-row report becomes empty, a multi-row report loses its first row, and an empty report throws instead of returning successfully.
findings.title: Return all report rows instead of skipping the first

findings.body: The replacement assertion checks only that a list exists, so it cannot detect dropped or reordered rows. This removes the content-preservation check precisely when the implementation changes to slicing the list. Restore the exact-content assertion and add an empty-input case to cover the new boundary behavior.

findings.body: Concatenating `user` into a `sh -c` command allows shell metacharacters and command substitutions to execute rather than being treated as literal username characters. If a caller controls `user`, they can execute arbitrary commands with the application's privileges. Restore direct execution with a separate argument.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies `alice; touch /tmp/report-injected` as user; the shell runs both the report command and the attacker's command with the application's privileges.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection by passing user as an argument

findings.body: `rows[1:]` discards the first row for every nonempty input, contradicting the stated goal of preserving report rows. It also panics for nil slices or empty slices with zero capacity. Returning `rows` preserves the contents and supports these boundary cases.
findings.failure_scenario: A named user with one report row receives an empty result; a nil rows argument instead causes a slice-bounds panic.
findings.title: Return all rows without slicing away the first entry

findings.body: The replacement assertion only checks whether the result is nil, removing coverage of row count and the first row precisely when the return expression changes. Restore the preservation checks and add empty and nil input cases so the changed slicing behavior is exercised at its boundaries.
findings.title: Restore assertions on row contents and cover empty input

ground_truth.commit_message: feat: preserve report rows for named users
